$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186205228 :tutorial/content "Now, let's consider the following linear congruence:

*Let $a$, $b,$ and $n$ integers. If $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1$, then the linear congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n)$  has a unique solution.*

**Proof**.  

To prove this theorem, we must show that a solution exists and that it is unique. 

First, we prove that a solution exists:

- If $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1$, then by Bézout's identity, there exist integers $u$ and $v$ such that 

$$
au+nv=1.
$$

We can write this result in modulo $n$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}au+nv & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,n) \\ au & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

 
This means that $u$ is the multiplicative inverse of $a$ (modulo $n$).

So, multiplying both sides of the original congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n)$ by $u,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & ≡b &  & (\text{mod}\,n) \\ u\cdot ax & ≡u\cdot b &  & (\text{mod}\,n) \\ (u\cdot a)x & ≡ub &  & (\text{mod}\,n) \\ 1\cdot x & ≡ub &  & (\text{mod}\,n) \\ x & ≡ub &  & (\text{mod}\,n)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x \equiv ub \: (\text{mod}\:n)$ is a solution.

Next, we prove the solution is unique:

- To prove uniqueness, we show that two solutions $x_1$ and $x_2$ to our congruence must be congruent. 

Suppose $x_1$ and $x_2$ are two solutions to the congruence, i.e., $ax_1 \equiv b\: (\textrm{mod}\,{n})$ and $ax_2 \equiv b\:  (\textrm{mod}\,{n})$. We want to show that $x_1 \equiv x_2$.

Since $ax_1 \equiv b\:  (\textrm{mod}\,{n})$ and $ax_2 \equiv b\:  (\textrm{mod}\,{n})$, we have

$$
ax_1 \equiv ax_2  \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,{n}).
$$

Now, since $\text{gcd}(a,n) = 1$, we can multiply both sides by the modular inverse of $a$ modulo $n ,$ which we previously denoted $u.$ 

$$
(u \cdot a) x_1 \equiv (u \cdot a) x_2  \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,{n})
$$

Since $a$ and $n$ are relatively prime, $u$ exists. Therefore, $u \cdot a \equiv 1\:(\textrm{mod}\,{n})$, and we have

$$
x_1 \equiv x_2  \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,{n}),
$$

as required.

Thus, we have shown both the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the congruence $ax \equiv b \pmod{n}$ when $\text{gcd}(a,n) = 1$." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186204121 :activity/expected-seconds 1020.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$15x≡4\,(\text{mod}\,43).$"] ["question-6fe75766-c260-5668-9726-1bdf3c8f2f17" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a linear congruence $ax≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and $$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(15,43)=1.

First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}43 & = & 15\cdot 2 & + & 13 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 15 & = & 13\cdot 1 & + & 2 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 13 & = & 2\cdot 6 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}13 & =43-15\cdot 2 \\ 2 & =15-13 \\ 1 & =13-2\cdot 6.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =13-2\cdot 6 \\  & =13-(15-13)\cdot 6 \\  & =13\cdot 7-15\cdot 6 \\  & =(43-15\cdot 2)\cdot 7-15\cdot 6 \\  & =43\cdot 7-15\cdot 20 \\  & =43\cdot 7+15\cdot (-20)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
1=43\cdot 7+15\cdot (-20).
$$

We can write this result in modulo $43,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}43\cdot 7+15\cdot (-20) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,43) \\ 15\cdot (-20) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,43) \\ 15\cdot (43-20) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,43) \\ 15\cdot 23 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,43)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $15\cdot 23≡1\,(\text{mod}\,43),$ which means that $23$ is the multiplicative inverse of $15$ (modulo $43$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $23,$ we get the following:

$$

$$

following theorem:

> *Let $a$, $b$, and $n$ integers. If $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1$, then the linear congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n)$ has a unique solution.*

**Proof**.

To prove this theorem, we must show that a solution exists and that it is unique.

First, we prove that a solution exists:

- If $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1$, then by Bézout's identity, there exist integers $u$ and $v$ such that
$au+nv=1$.
We can write this result in modulo $n$ as follows:
$\begin{bmatrix}au + nv & ≡1 & (modn) \\ au & ≡1 & (modn)\end{bmatrix}$
This means that $u$ is the multiplicative inverse of $a$ (modulo $n$).So, multiplying both sides of the original congruence $ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n)$ by $u$, we get
$\begin{bmatrix}ax & ≡b & (modn) \\ u \cdot ax & ≡u \cdot b & (modn) \\ (u \cdot a)x & ≡ub & (modn) \\ 1 \cdot x & ≡ub & (modn) \\ x & ≡ub & (modn)\end{bmatrix}$
Therefore, $x \equiv ub \: (\text{mod}\:n)$ is a solution.

Next, we prove the solution is unique:

- To prove uniqueness, we show that two solutions $x_1$ and $x_2$ to our congruence must be congruent. Suppose $x_1$ and $x_2$ are two solutions to the congruence, i.e., $ax_1 \equiv b\: (\textrm{mod}\,{n})$ and $ax_2 \equiv b\: (\textrm{mod}\,{n})$. We want to show that $x_1 \equiv x_2$.Since $ax_1 \equiv b\: (\textrm{mod}\,{n})$ and $ax_2 \equiv b\: (\textrm{mod}\,{n})$, we have
$ax_1 \equiv ax_2 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,{n})$.Now, since $\text{gcd}(a,n) = 1$, we can multiply both sides by the modular inverse of $a$ modulo $n$, which we previously denoted $u$.
$(u \cdot a) x_1 \equiv (u \cdot a) x_2 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,{n})$Since $a$ and $n$ are relatively prime, $u$ exists. Therefore, $u \cdot a \equiv 1\:(\textrm{mod}\,{n})$, and we have
$x_1 \equiv x_2 \qquad (\textrm{mod}\,{n})$,
as required.

Thus, we have shown both the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the congruence $ax \equiv b \pmod{n}$ when

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n) = 1
$$
